describe? The parent builds a fixed 1024-byte record from its own original
context, signed-document digests, actual images, streams, guardians and closed
census. In particular, the config identity names its sealed runtime copy, not
the source inode. The existing legacy record is compared against its original
private token/bindings; the new record receives its digest, not an exported token.

Seals prevent content changes but do not prove that truthful content was sealed.
The portable decoder therefore returns assertions, never a permit. It can accept
a shape-valid mutation; the parent's exact expected-byte comparison must reject
that mutation. Private memfd tests exercise bytes/inode/offset/seals, while
modeled original contexts exercise field mapping. Neither proves child identity
or execution, and no child is started by these checks.

The new retained role sits inside the same old full frames, without changing
their count/order or the absolute admission windows. Losing a retained record
refuses rather than silently manufacturing a replacement. Additional hashing
and metadata work is bounded but unmeasured: passing unit tests does not show
that full original preparation fits its deadline. A separately authenticated
child-reader/executable, actual original delivery and writer-death proof remain
the next execution gates; an immutable assertion is only a prerequisite.

### A child reader must reject a well formed forgery as authority

The [separate bootstrap executable](../testing/performance/0.74/bootstrap-child-reader-20261023.md)
now reads the fixed entry through bounded positional reads, checking exact size,
readonly state, seals, metadata and offset before comparing a second observation.
It neither repairs its inputs nor changes the parent's validation windows. Child
descriptor flags differ deliberately from parent retention flags: an inherited
descriptor cannot still have CLOEXEC set across the exec that delivered it.

The important negative control is not a corrupt byte. It is a completely
canonical, sealed record with invented ownership data. The reader can establish
that those assertions were read consistently, but cannot establish their truth.
The executable therefore exits at an explicit authentication-closed boundary,
including for that forged input. This separates actual kernel input checks from
the still-required original credentials, manager/root/guardians and complete FD
authentication. Compiling the selected bootstrap is similarly distinct from
enrolling its exact signed build. Neither result permits launcher execution,
writer completion or a server rehearsal.

### A complete descriptor census is not proof of original ownership

The [complete bootstrap census](../testing/performance/0.74/bootstrap-child-census-20261023.md)
now checks all fifteen named roles against the entry and rejects additional
inherited descriptors. Inspecting only the expected slots would leave a hidden
writer outside the apparent inventory. The bounded procfs enumeration therefore
matters independently of image hashes, stream identities, release credentials,
pidfd liveness and the existing absolute alarm.

The negative control also becomes stronger: a fresh child receives a complete,
consistent set of private kernel resources rather than an entry file alone.
Those resources can agree with invented claims, so passing their consistency
checks still ends at authentication-closed. Ordinary owned helper pidfds do not
become privileged guardians, and a closed FD set in one process does not revoke
copies elsewhere. Original manager/root and actual credential/build provenance
remain necessary before launcher execution or writer completion.

The old entry-only mode and parent frames remain exact; new checks never refresh
the original deadline. Their added hashing/procfs/clock-query cost is unmeasured.
These correctness controls cannot supply a throughput claim or prove full
original admission fits its window.

Final local correctness controls passed on Windows, GNU 1.94 and GNU MSRV 1.88;
the component report links exact source snapshots and logs, including the first
lint, registry and Windows executable-lock failures. Their later corrections
are not evidence of faster preparation: there was no measurement cohort or
original live retry. Even the successfully compiled unsigned bootstrap needs a
clean-source signed build and independent enrollment before it can be trusted.

### Identical executable bytes do not identify the original image

The next [current executable check](../testing/performance/0.74/bootstrap-current-image-20261023.md)
addresses a gap left by a complete descriptor census: the supplied bootstrap
image may agree with its entry while another inode executes. The new opt-in
mode compares readonly sealed FD13 with fixed procfs executable lookup, including
the entire metadata stamp and zero offsets. It repeats this fresh observation
around the unchanged census revalidation; temporary inspection FDs close before
the census so they cannot become unexplained inherited resources.

Two sealed files with identical contents remain distinct in the unit control.
Process controls distinguish a matching sealed diagnostic image from the same
bytes supplied alongside an on-disk executable; that latter image also lacks
memfd seals, so the process case alone cannot isolate inode equality. Crucially,
even the matching sealed image with a complete forged context reaches only the
explicit authentication-closed boundary. Content and inode consistency cannot
select the policy that should trust them.

Windows, GNU 1.94 and MSRV 1.88 correctness gates passed with original live frames
and admission origins unchanged. Procfs namespace enrollment, actual credentials,
signed build selection and original manager/root/guardian provenance still need
their independent join before launcher handoff. No timing or throughput cohort
was run: added kernel queries have not been shown to fit original admission
windows merely because synthetic correctness controls pass.

### The parent and sandbox child do not share one trust context

The [production child boundary audit](../testing/performance/0.74/bootstrap-child-boundary-audit-20261023.md)
found why the next step cannot be another equality check against the creator's
claims. Existing fixed trust openers require root, while the projected unit
selects the unprivileged hydracache-perf account and preserves filesystem
namespacing hardening. A same-host mount-namespace reader cannot enroll the
resulting child sandbox by assuming it shares the parent's namespace.

Executable origin is a separate prerequisite. Executing a private sealed
diagnostic copy proves that the image-consistency leaf works; it does not give
systemd an address for that inode. A normally installed bootstrap with identical
bytes is a different object, already rejected by the earlier control. Production
must explicitly distinguish its independently enrolled executable origin from
the sealed reference copy, or supply a reviewed FD-native addressing mechanism.

The proposed next contract keeps root-only selection and all sandbox properties,
then binds the particular held child's generation, namespaces, credentials,
image and streams under the original owner before release. It needs a versioned
inventory/authentication/replay design, not a fallback or a fresh admission
window. The user subsequently approved local implementation. This audit adds
source guards only; no production child, launcher handoff or performance
improvement is claimed.

### An installed bootstrap needs its own retained origin

The first [installed-origin implementation](../testing/performance/0.74/bootstrap-installed-origin-20261023.md)
keeps the original sealed reference instead of repurposing it. A consuming wrapper
retains the separately named installed image, compares its safe ancestry and
exact inode/metadata/content with the same owner's verified bootstrap build,
and repeats those observations between the unchanged complete bootstrap frames.
The installed object and sealed reference must be distinct even when their
content hashes match. Neither object selects the key or policy that trusts it.

The parent-local inventory accounts for every added descriptor: four ancestry
handles and the installed image extend the old 27 to 32, while semantic roles
grow from fifteen to sixteen. Same-byte name replacement, aliases, unsafe modes,
flags/offset drift or missing retained source refuse without replacement or
retry. On failure the original owner retires before the new descriptors close.

Private filesystem controls and owner models check this read-only composition,
not an installed production binary or a live child admission. The next protocol
must bind the actual sandbox executable/credentials/namespaces to that retained
origin before release. Additional pathname walks and content hashing may affect
preparation cost, but correctness test elapsed time supplies no performance or
original-deadline-fit claim.

Review tightened the new ancestry contract to require search permission for the
future non-root child, not just the privileged reader. The initial private-root
controls and the first strict lint refusals remain in the evidence alongside
corrected final checks. Nine new filesystem/census/owner controls and the selected
preceding Linux controls passed on GNU 1.94 and MSRV 1.88; these observations remain
separate from real root-host enrollment, current-child authentication and the
actual systemd execution gate.

### Entry consistency cannot replace original owner authentication

The separate [installed-entry schema](../testing/performance/0.74/bootstrap-installed-entry-20261023.md)
expresses the new origin without changing the old sealed-reference record. Its
1280-byte envelope embeds the original 1024 bytes and separately describes the
installed device/inode/size, content hash, fixed pathname and asserted parent
inventory fingerprint. Matching content must coexist with different image
identities; equal hash is not permission to reinterpret the old inode check.

The codec tests corruption and canonical representation, not throughput. Every
single-bit mutation must either refuse or produce a different value that
re-encodes exactly. Cross-image mismatches and malformed embedded records refuse
even when their unkeyed checksums are recomputed. Such checksums catch inconsistent
assertions; they cannot prove who supplied a fully consistent forged record.

That distinction is explicit in a positive parsing control with invented owner,
documents, origins and inventory. The next integration must not treat successful
decoding as authenticated custody. Production must derive and retain
the record under the same original owner, then observe/admit the actual sandbox
child before release. This component adds no fresh live query, transport or
execution and makes no preparation-cost or original-deadline-fit claim.

### Materialization must retain the original owner and exclude self reference

The [installed-entry materialization](../testing/performance/0.74/bootstrap-installed-material-20261023.md)
now consumes the original installed owner instead of accepting a canonical record
from a caller. The factory reads its retained old sealed entry under stamp and
census brackets, combines it with the same installed inventory, and retains a
new readonly/CLOEXEC/four-sealed memfd. The old complete validator still brackets
two inspections with three installed-owner frames. More work may affect deadline
fit; synthetic correctness test elapsed time cannot establish that fit.

The input inventory and resulting inventory differ deliberately. HCBI0741 asserts
the existing 32-descriptor/sixteen-role prefix. Retaining the new record adds one
descriptor and role, making the resulting parent inventory 33/17. Hashing that
result back into its own record would create a circular dependency. A separately
labelled fingerprint therefore covers the input values and stamps only; it is
not a child slot map or authenticated message.

The wrapper cannot reconstruct missing retained material after successful
construction. An observation failure remains a refusal even after restoring an
inode, flags or offset. The same refused owner and published record stay held
through the error; explicit retirement precedes descriptor closure. Internal
construction temporaries retain their existing cleanup, and a sealed memory
record is not durable lifecycle completion. This local owner composition still
does not prove live child enrollment, original delivery or writer cessation.

### The current executable and its reference have different jobs

The [installed-child consistency reader](../testing/performance/0.74/bootstrap-installed-child-20261023.md)
now checks the installed inode separately from its sealed content reference.
An explicit versioned mode requires the original fifteen roles plus the
installed image and sealed installed-entry assertion. A new bounded closed-set
checker accepts precisely those child slots; the original fifteen-role capture
and its predicates are reused unchanged, rather than relaxing the old checker.

The installed entry must embed the separately observed old entry bytes exactly.
The installed file's full hash agrees with the sealed reference, while fixed
procfs executable lookup must identify the installed file's actual inode and
complete metadata. The complete observation repeats. Equal bytes at a different
current inode refuse before the authentication boundary, but matching all of
these assertions does not establish who supplied them or which host namespace
gave them meaning. A matching forged owned executable still exits with original
authentication closed. Root selection remains in the unchanged original parent;
this leaf is not independent root/policy or sandbox enrollment.

The process controls also exposed an evidence-quality gap. The first MSRV fault
control saw shell exit 126, but its exit assertion preceded stderr collection.
Its exact inner fault and errno are consequently unknown and remain recorded as
unknown. The corrected helper captures bounded stderr first and labels the fault.
Serialized filesystem fixture controls avoid overlapping executable writers and
forks; a deliberately held writer separately demonstrates Text file busy and
shell exit 126 without entering the reader. That control explains a possible
failure class, not the unsaved cause of the first failure.

The source contracts caught two smaller integration mistakes: module ordering
rejected by formatting, then added whitespace left after removing the new hook.
Both first refusals stay in the packet. Only new integration text changed; exact
views still restore complete old bodies. Windows source contracts and selected
GNU/MSRV component controls, strict lint and local metadata gates now pass on one
source snapshot. These are correctness observations, not faster preparation or
evidence of fitting the original admission windows. Actual sandbox admission
under the same manager, original delivery and cessation of every writer remain
the next integration boundary before completion or server execution can open.

### Bind observations through the original owner rather than caller snapshots

The [sandbox observer composition](../testing/performance/0.74/bootstrap-sandbox-owner-20261023.md)
now takes only the consumed original installed-entry owner. It derives the unit,
attempt cgroup, installed image, streams, worker credentials and original bounds
from that same authenticated context. Fixed queries use its retained manager
connection and unique manager name; there is no PID argument, alternate manager
snapshot or independently supplied namespace number to promote into trust.

The selected MainPID is pinned with proc generation documents and a pidfd. The
new reader keeps the sandbox mount namespace distinct from the original host
policy mount namespace, while user/PID/time namespaces must share the enrolled
observer's context. Actual executable, pipe objects and exclusive cgroup
population must agree under repeated observations. The old same-host namespace
API remains unchanged. The wrapper uses three complete original validations
around two manager/kernel observations; no timestamp or deadline is renewed.

Credential review illustrates why stronger-looking code is not automatically a
faithful implementation. The existing contract requires zero active capability
sets and NoNewPrivs, and pins the first observed bounding set against drift. It
does not require an empty bounding set, and the unchanged unit does not clear it.
The new observer's initial zero-bounding condition was corrected to that existing
rule before fixed checks. This changes no old guard or acceptance threshold.

The local gate covers ownership/order/fault models, manager reply and value
rules, bounded parsing and a real owned helper that cannot substitute its foreign
cgroup or ordinary namespace for the sandbox. GNU/MSRV checks and strict lint
passed; a positive original-manager sandbox was not run under the no-service
scope. The object deliberately grants observation only. Seeing a matching
pre-existing unit is not proof that this owner delivered its creation request;
complete loaded-unit settings, authenticated child enrollment and original
delivery still precede release, writer cessation and completion. Additional
validation cost remains unmeasured, not an implied preparation improvement.

### Delivery and readiness have separate irreversible boundaries

The [held-delivery candidate](../testing/performance/0.74/bootstrap-held-delivery-20261023.md)
now retains a newly addressed message under the consumed installed-entry owner.
It does not reinterpret the historical two-output-FD worker request. The held
message preserves the original serial and projected hardening, chooses only the
fixed installed bootstrap and adds a distinct readiness endpoint to the seventeen
original roles. Its FD aliases remain owned through uncertainty or refusal.
This wire construction is separate from successful installation or service start.

The extra endpoint follows from an existing invariant, not a convenience. Every
old full material frame requires the release socket to be empty. Sending a
handshake over it would either fail those checks or tempt an implementation to
skip them. Readiness traffic therefore uses a separate socket, while all old
release checks remain intact. Parent operations retain the full owner frame and
manager/process observation; challenge and job correlation retain the original
absolute bound rather than starting a new allowance.

Both send windows become uncertain before their first possible send. A missing
job reply does not prove that the manager did nothing. Likewise a missing child
acknowledgement does not authorize a repeated challenge. Readiness binds a fresh
nonce to the installed-entry digest, original context, unique manager/client,
invocation, creator, selected child and absolute deadline. The checksum is not a
signature: message authentication comes from kernel-delivered credentials and
an atomically received live pidfd, combined with the original parent's checks.
A socket's creation-time peer credentials cannot substitute for the sender of
each later message.

Local owned-helper controls exercise this exchange without a service or product
workload. They remain narrower than original delivery through systemd. At that
stage the eighteen-role child entry and activation environment were not connected;
the following gate adds readiness only, while old installed modes still refuse.
A manager job observation and readiness
are deliberately not a worker-release capability, durable completion or proof
that every writer has stopped. No preparation speedup or fit within the original
windows is inferred from these correctness controls.

The first retained GNU check passed the new component controls but hit a rustc
diagnostic-rendering ICE while reporting intentionally unconnected child code.
The next GNU/MSRV checks reached strict lint, which rejected a large owner enum,
a large error return and the deliberate second compilation of the frozen private
ancillary leaf. The correction boxes the large owner/error values and explicitly
labels that parser reuse; the original parser remains byte-for-byte unchanged.
Both copies now run their malformed-record and FD-cleanup controls. Reviewed
local gates pass, while all earlier refused lanes remain separate evidence.
None of these compiler/layout corrections establishes an allocation improvement
or changes an admission threshold.

### Child readiness does not authorize execution

The [eighteen-role entry](../testing/performance/0.74/bootstrap-held-entry-20261023.md)
now checks the inherited role set before answering its separate readiness
challenge. The old seventeen-role mode stays intact. Its new activation contract
accepts only the current canonical PID fields, fifteen exact names, descriptor
count and invocation identifier; these values describe activation, not authority.
The parent suppresses a finite list of manager defaults, and the child refuses
unknown environment rather than silently making an unexpected launch look valid.

The reader retains every old role predicate and observation order. Only the new
readiness endpoint changes to CLOEXEC before ownership. Full fresh role frames
run before receiving the challenge, after receipt and after the sole possible
ACK. After that ACK the process only waits under its original creator/guardian
pidfds, alarm and channel. Expiry, disconnect or duplicate data stops readiness;
there is no release-channel write or worker exec. This preserves the distinction
between proving readiness and gaining permission to do work.

The first integration failure was informative about the fixtures. Older
consistency-only records used identical manager and client hashes. Such a record
can be structurally valid, but the readiness protocol correctly rejects it. The
new fixture supplies distinct endpoints and reseals its matching assertions;
neither the runtime predicate nor its deadline changed. A separate negative
control retains the old equal-name refusal. A passing parser fixture therefore
does not automatically become a passing authentication fixture.

The lost-ACK check found another important boundary. A packet can remain queued
after its sender dies without remaining an authenticated live-sender observation.
An attempted late receive after SIGKILL/reap returned Invalid on the local WSL
kernel. Both GNU and MSRV first failures remain in evidence. The corrected oracle
peeks at the exact queued ACK while the child is alive, leaves it unconsumed,
kills and reaps that same child, verifies its held pidfd is dead and requires the
late refusal. It does not relax the ancillary parser to recover permission from
old bytes. The alarm control likewise checks the original timerfd without rearming
it. All original admission windows remain unchanged.

The local matrix now covers valid readiness, malformed activation and roles,
context or sender substitution, duplicate challenge, guardian loss, disconnect,
expiry and owned-child SIGKILL. Source contracts also restore entire old bodies
to their Git baseline. These correctness results are not preparation-speed or
throughput measurements. Original delivery through the real manager, complete
unit hardening, authenticated worker start and all-writer cessation before fence
release still require their own integration gates. No service, clock or server
action was needed for this readiness-only gate.

### A status query can be the wrong absence test

The next [original-manager experiment](../testing/performance/0.74/bootstrap-original-service-20261023.md)
connects the real consumed owner to the diagnostic installed image and its
readiness-only transport. It deliberately does not recycle the old fixture's
private cgroup mount: systemd must place any child on its actual tree. Production
frames and original admission windows are unchanged; no worker can be released.

The first result was not a successful delivery. Debian first rejected an account
preparation option, before libtest invocation. The compatible candidate then entered
the original-owner test once and stopped at the unit-absence guard. There were
zero causal observations, no scope creation and no manager send. A read-only
control explained why: systemctl show can report an implicit slice definition as
loaded even when GetUnit says the unit is not loaded. A status/property lookup is
not interchangeable with a non-loading existence query.

The isolated correction uses GetUnit and recognizes only the exact missing-unit
response. Permission failures, disconnects, a different unit or extra output are
uncertainty, not permission to create. GNU and MSRV controls cover these cases;
the first live refusal is not replaced by a rerun. This is a preflight correction,
not a cheaper validation frame or a measured runtime improvement.

WSL supplied another lesson: a shared VM boot_id can remain unchanged across a
distro init that replaces the mount namespace and clears tmpfs /tmp. Recovery
data must outlive that boundary. The runner now keeps protected recovery copies
in /var/tmp, and compares the account entries and diagnostic inode it actually
owns. Cleanup succeeded for the original-test candidate, but cleanup does not
prove the untouched all-writer retirement protocol. Real delivery, readiness,
retirement, completion and server admission still need separate positive gates.

### A clock ordering refusal is not a preparation timeout

The separately authorized [GetUnit original-owner attempt](../testing/performance/0.74/bootstrap-original-getunit-20261023.md)
passed the corrected absence check and created its own transient slice. That
progress did not establish delivery: the same unchanged runtime then refused at
live kernel revalidation before causal/consent frames or a service request. Its
first failure and successful owned cleanup are retained independently from the
earlier absence failure; no repeat was used to turn the result green.

The saved samples explain the immediate predicate. With the same boot identifier,
BOOTTIME advanced 1.450720029 seconds, while the later REALTIME observation was
4.572444734 seconds earlier. The unchanged ordering check rejects that pair before
the unchanged sixty-second hold budget could admit it. Making preparation faster
or enlarging a timeout would not demonstrate that these time observations are
consistent. The trace alone does not identify a particular service, WSL mechanism
or vDSO/CPU behavior as the underlying cause.

This experiment therefore confirms a narrower result: the non-loading preflight
works on the actual manager, and the live clock guard remains fail-closed. It
does not confirm original delivery, readiness or all-writer cessation. Clock
consistency needs read-only attribution before another recorded live candidate;
the first refusal, original origins and every existing predicate remain intact.

### Masked services do not prove independent WSL clocks

A [read-only clock observation](../testing/performance/0.74/wsl-clock-readonly-20261023.md)
removed the admission workflow from the experiment. One fixed session collected
601 low-rate rows, bracketing direct kernel clock_gettime reads with libc reads.
REALTIME went backwards twice through both paths, by about 5.93 seconds between
adjacent rows. BOOTTIME and MONOTONIC kept increasing; boot, init and namespace
identities did not change within the session. The problem is therefore observable
without original-owner preparation and is not confined to libc observations.

The environment supplied a useful boundary correction. Clock services were
masked inside the diagnostic distro, but a separate read-only query found an
active systemd-timesyncd in Ubuntu with the same VM boot ID and time namespace.
Kernel metadata also recorded a configured implicit time-sync mechanism and earlier
backward-time messages. These facts expose possible shared-clock authorities;
they do not identify which mechanism caused either sampled step. Disabling a
service based only on this association would confuse a candidate with a cause.

The direct MONOTONIC and RAW endpoint differences also disagreed, so diagnosing
the time setter alone may not explain all observed rate behavior. The raw series,
first anomaly and failed Windows time-status query are retained separately from
the original admission refusal. No clocks, services, predicates or deadlines
changed, and original-owner was not repeated. This is progress in attribution,
not a successful delivery gate or a preparation-speed improvement.

### A synchronized status can hide an abnormal kernel tick

The next [read-only attribution](../testing/performance/0.74/wsl-clock-causality-20261023.md)
found a concrete explanation for the MONOTONIC/RAW disagreement. All 81 kernel
queries returned tick=9167 microseconds instead of the nominal 10000, alongside
a much smaller frequency adjustment. Their combined rate prediction falls
inside the observed RAW-bracketed range. Looking only at the frequency field or
a synchronized status would miss the coarse adjustment that dominates this
series. RAW is a comparison clock here, not a certified UTC reference.

The same series separates correction paths. New NTP responses reported positive
offsets near 8.786 seconds; one forward clock residual closely matched its
response offset. A different interval moved REALTIME backwards without a new
NTP packet, temporarily adding STA_UNSYNC. The enabled Hyper-V path is a plausible
opposing setter, but neither that bit nor a configured driver uniquely identifies
the caller. Existing audit and trace records were empty, so the historical writer
of tick and exact backward setter remain unresolved.

These findings matter operationally: a time-service state is not a complete
clock-state measurement, and explaining a rate does not identify who configured
it. The first metadata permission failure was retained, then a separate collector
read the complete root context while every modes=0 query remained unprivileged.
No clock, service, runtime predicate or admission window changed. There is no
reason to turn an environmental timing finding into a weaker original-owner
guard or a successful server gate.

### Publication order limits a clock correlation

An [offline audit of the retained series](../testing/performance/0.74/wsl-clock-offline-join-20261023.md)
made the acquisition geometry explicit: each clock read preceded its NTP getter.
A response first seen in one row may have been applied after that row's clock
read. Comparing only adjacent same-row values can therefore attach too much
precision to an apparent event match.

Extending each comparison through the following clock sample preserves the
large opposing remainders for two packets, conditional on successful NTP step
application. It does not turn an arithmetic remainder into an observed syscall
or certify nanosecond clock accuracy. The audit reproduces the original analysis
without replacing it and uses no new live observations. The next attribution
boundary is explicit: enabling a bounded trace needs separate authorization,
and even a successful future trace cannot recover a historical tick writer
that does not write again.

### A failed trace must not become a successful attribution

An explicitly approved [bounded WSL trace](../testing/performance/0.74/wsl-clock-trace-20261023.md)
attempted to distinguish clock-setting paths using private-instance events,
typed kernel arguments, return values and stacks. The hypothesis was that
actual setter calls could separate the opposing correction from the NTP
service correlation. That hypothesis was not tested successfully: configuration
returned EINVAL before a usable trace or query series existed.

The useful confirmed result is narrower. A guardian armed before instrumentation
and the normal cleanup path both reported removal of the owned instance/probes;
global tracing controls and session identities stayed unchanged. The attempt
was sealed as a failure, without a second live dispatch or an original-owner
retry. No performance improvement, absent writer or healthy delivery is claimed.

The refusal also exposed a collector defect: retaining only the exception text
discarded the failing operation's location. A separate source-only correction
now retains the exact control path and traceback, with negative tests for both
buffered write and close failures. It was not used to rewrite the old result or
silently repeat the observation. Instrumentation needs failure diagnostics and
its own cleanup tests; product guards and admission windows must not absorb the
cost of making an experiment appear successful. Setter attribution remains
open, and another bounded capture is a separate authorization boundary.

### Append streams can fail before a virtual file receives a command

The separately approved [configuration diagnostic](../testing/performance/0.74/wsl-clock-einval-20261023.md)
localized the failure without another clock series. A durable before/after
journal showed that instance creation, buffer size, trace clock and stacktrace
setup worked. Opening the probe registry as a Python append stream then failed
before the first definition was written. A parser or function-address change
would therefore target a stage this attempt never reached.

The source-level explanation is a mismatch between regular-file append
semantics and a virtual control interface. CPython seeks to the end during
append-stream construction; this registry uses seq_lseek, which rejects that
seek with EINVAL. The exact open failure was observed; the intervening syscall
was explained from the pinned implementations, not recorded in a syscall trace.

A future command writer must avoid implicit seeks without adding O_TRUNC.
Changing the mode to `w` would be unsafe because opening this registry with
truncation releases probe definitions. The correct boundary is an isolated
non-seeking, non-truncating writer with full-command and short-write checks,
followed by separately scoped live validation. The diagnostic stopped on its
first failure, cleaned its private instance, preserved the earlier archive and
left clocks, services, runtime checks and admission windows unchanged. It fixes
the direction of the next experiment, not the unobserved clock-setting cause.

### A command writer and a receipt reader need different completion proofs

The [isolated collector correction](../testing/performance/0.74/wsl-clock-writer-20261023.md)
now sends one registry command without a high-level append stream. Exact flags
exclude creation and truncation, no seek occurs, and a short write refuses
without resubmitting a possibly applied command. Mock syscall checks and owned
regular-file controls cover both registration and deletion payloads. They do
not prove that the pinned kernel accepts those registrations.

The first complete local suite exposed a different completion mistake in an
existing SIGKILL test. File creation made the guardian receipt visible before
its JSON write had finished, so the reader sometimes parsed an empty file.
The production collector already waits for its guardian child; the failing
orphan-process test instead waited only for file existence. A separate
test-harness fix signals after the real write/flush/fsync and reads once, with
the same four-second limit. A deterministic empty-file control covers the race.

Both the old writer's regression refusal and the first suite error remain
archived. The corrected 31-control result belongs to the explicit source/method
change, not to repeated unchanged trials. No live probes or clock series ran.
The common lesson is concrete: a submitted command needs a checked completion
boundary, and a visible receipt needs a proven publication boundary. Neither
justifies weakening product guards or declaring a later server gate successful.

### Real registration is a narrower gate than a useful trace

The [fresh WSL configuration gate](../testing/performance/0.74/wsl-clock-registration-20261023.md)
confirmed that the corrected writer can register all seven exact probes on the
pinned kernel and remove them afterward. All 28 journaled setup operations
completed, with the private buffer disabled throughout. The same preflight,
guardian and deadline checks were reused, and root controls/session identities
matched after retirement. Earlier failures remain archived independently.

This result removes the observed append-stream blocker for the tested
registration path. It does not validate the values emitted by running probes,
the stack decoder or loss counters, because no events or clock samples were
collected. Separating configuration from observation makes the next question
precise: can one bounded capture identify the opposing setter while retaining
complete loss and cleanup evidence? A configuration pass is neither that
capture nor permission to reopen an original-owner or server gate.

### Increasing samples can hide opposing clock setters

The [bounded setter capture](../testing/performance/0.74/wsl-clock-setter-20261023.md)
finally observed actual call paths: chronyd tick/frequency adjustments, absolute
settime calls from tasks named init, and positive timesyn offset injections.
Paired returns and kernel stacks distinguish these from mere entry requests.
Zero loss counters and kprobe misses support this finite capture, not a claim
that every possible clock-setting path was instrumented.

The 161 helper samples were all increasing in REALTIME. Nevertheless, three
successful absolute targets were earlier than their preceding sample, followed
quickly by roughly +8.82-second offset injections in the same intervals. The
resulting helper residuals were positive, around +2.74 seconds. Sampling alone
would therefore hide the opposing activity. Offline arithmetic reproduces the
windows on the first sealed bytes; it is not a measurement of each isolated
step with nanosecond accuracy.

The trace also observed the current coarse tick writer instead of inferring it
from the resulting rate. That does not identify the writer of an older value:
the new tick/frequency pair differs from the previous read-only series. Nor is
a kernel PID an authenticated service identity. A visible Ubuntu lookup of 210
was agetty, not the trace's chronyd task, so assigning a distribution or service
from the numeric PID would be unsound. The next decision needs namespace-aware
identity evidence and an agreed clock policy, not a wider admission window.

All probes and the private instance were retired, original tracing controls and
session identities matched, and the earlier failures remained intact. No
clock/service change or product/server execution followed this observation.

### PID numbers need a namespace and an observation boundary

The following [read-only namespace audit](../testing/performance/0.74/wsl-clock-writer-identity-20261023.md)
identified the currently visible Ubuntu timesyncd executable without changing
its service. System-distro PID 193 and Ubuntu PID 176 share start ticks, the
executable digest, credentials, cgroup and target namespaces. The NSpid chain
`193 176` explains how the same current process appears in both procfs views.
This is stronger than matching a comm string, but still weaker than binding the
process to the earlier trace: kernel PID 1157's original start ticks and
executable were not captured.

Numeric lookups demonstrate the danger. Ubuntu PID 210 is agetty, whereas the
trace's kernel PID 210 issued chronyd adjustments. Docker PID 1157 is a loki
thread, not the trace's timesyn identity. Neither collision says that a writer
changed executable. They say that a bare PID from one namespace cannot be
looked up in another as though the identity were global. A later executable
digest also cannot retroactively authenticate the writer of an older value.

Root-namespace access is the remaining concrete metadata boundary. Microsoft's
documented debug shell refused because the Windows caller was not elevated;
the refusal remains evidence rather than triggering an elevation workaround or
a new capture. Current chronyd ownership therefore remains unresolved. Disabling
only the visible Ubuntu service would choose a policy before accounting for
all observed writers sharing the time namespace.

The metadata archive also caught a smaller portability defect: exact-byte
verification parsed CRLF fixture bytes differently from a text-mode read. The
first failed control stays sealed, and an isolated in-memory line-ending
correction has its own regression test. All 46 Linux controls now pass; runtime
checks and original windows remain unchanged. Better attribution narrows the
next intervention. It does not turn an infrastructure diagnosis into a product
performance improvement or permission to reopen original delivery.

### A diagnostic handoff must stop before an unavailable privilege

The [root-namespace runner](../testing/performance/0.74/wsl-clock-root-namespace-plan-20261023.md)
turns the remaining access boundary into a bounded operator action. A non-admin
Windows caller refuses before invoking WSL. An already elevated caller must
still satisfy committed-source, evidence-pin and running-distro guards; the
script then reads only the fixed original PID numbers. It neither asks for its
own elevation nor starts missing distributions to recreate an older context.

The runner preserves one first exchange, including timeout or missing completion
markers, without redispatch. Nine mocked controls, eleven existing offline
controls and a syntax-only shell check pass. The first two test errors were a
bytes-versus-text mock defect and remain archived separately. These controls
prove local orchestration behavior, not that the real root debug shell accepts
the stdin exchange. That compatibility and the process identity interpretation
remain the next live metadata gate. No clock, service or product intervention
is hidden inside the handoff, and no original admission window has changed.

### Preflight failures need a journal outside the preflight process

The original operator handoff produced no retained console output or output
directory. Its [outcome](../testing/performance/0.74/root-namespace-first-unconfirmed-20261023.json)
therefore remains unknown: absence of a receipt cannot identify an exit code,
prove that no command ran, or establish which prerequisite failed. A later
working candidate must not replace that missing first observation.

The [separate journal-first preparation](../testing/performance/0.74/wsl-clock-root-namespace-journal-plan-20261023.md)
moves capture outside Python. PowerShell reserves an exclusive directory and
opens stdout, stderr and launcher-error files before looking up the interpreter.
Concurrent pipe drains avoid blocking on one full stream while waiting for the
other, and write-through files retain received bytes before final child-exit
processing. Python startup/import failures are visible even if the collector
never imports; captured git output and chained subprocess errors are saved
without changing the original calls, checks or deadlines.

Native fake-payload controls immediately found a distinct launcher defect:
Windows PowerShell returned two interpreter matches, producing an invalid
Process.Start filename. The first failed controls and their exact sources remain
sealed; the correction selects one PATH result without fallback or retry. This
finding explains that fixture failure, not the lost operator output. At the end
of preparation all 32 offline controls passed, but no real replacement launch
was performed or authorized. Logging preparation improves diagnosability; it supplies no evidence
of healthy original delivery, clock-policy suitability or a throughput gain.

### A retained access refusal is not a successful root lookup

The [single authorized journaled invocation](../testing/performance/0.74/wsl-clock-root-namespace-logged-attempt-20261023.md)
then supplied the missing diagnostic boundary in a real process. Python started
and the preserved Administrator check refused before git preflight or WSL.
The outer journal retained the exact exit 1, failure phase and full traceback;
there was no retry or elevation workaround. This confirms capture of that early
failure, not root access, clock health or authenticated writer identity.

The earlier operator attempt still has an unknown exit code because its console
output was lost. The new, known access refusal cannot fill that historical gap.
The two outcomes remain separately pinned. Original checks and windows stayed
unchanged, and no clock, service or server action followed. Further diagnosis
needs a real elevated execution context and a separately scoped fresh attempt,
not weakening the guard or silently reusing the journal.

### A timeout can retain useful data without becoming a passing run

The [separately approved UAC attempt](../testing/performance/0.74/wsl-clock-root-namespace-uac-attempt-20261023.md)
reached the root debug shell, but the unchanged 30-second client limit expired.
Python exited 1 and the collector kept its synthetic timeout result. Redirected
stdout still retained 18,864 bytes with the complete fixed metadata sequence.
Transport completion and useful observations are separate facts: keeping the
metadata does not justify replacing the timeout, extending the deadline or
running again until a green result appears.

The first offline audit made the opposite mistake: it assumed no stdout existed
because TimeoutExpired exposed no captured-output attributes. Those attributes
were empty because the call wrote to an open file rather than a PIPE. Reading
the original file corrected the analysis without another live observation. Both
the failed assertion and its source remain alongside the raw terminal bytes;
eight byte-only controls protect the corrected interpretation, including a
refusal to relabel the timeout as success. Prompts and echoed printf commands
are not accepted as standalone completion markers.

The root view narrows the clock investigation. Current PID 210 is the root
chronyd executable, not Ubuntu's numerically colliding agetty. Current PID 1157
has NSpid `1157 193 176`, matching the saved system-distro and Ubuntu timesyncd
views by start ticks, executable digest, credentials, namespaces and cgroup.
The three init numbers from the earlier trace resolve to threads of TGID 912,
not three independent service owners. All share the observed time namespace.
These are later identity observations, not retroactive authentication of the
trace: its start/executable context was not captured at the setter calls.

The end marker, logout text and equal distro inventory also do not prove that
every guest process retired after the Windows client timed out. That remains a
separate boundary, as do a clock-policy decision and healthy original delivery.
The useful outcome is a narrower diagnosis with an intact first refusal, not a
product-performance improvement or permission to change services. No original
window was widened and no clock, service or server intervention followed.

### Match the completion contract before adding another timeout workaround

The [offline transport review](../testing/performance/0.74/wsl-debug-transport-audit-20261023.md)
found a methodological mismatch. In the [reviewed WSL release source](https://github.com/microsoft/WSL/blob/642331364dda7a3d88bf64acb87e7056918a5fc9/src/windows/common/WslClient.cpp#L1367-L1413),
debug-shell is a named-pipe console relay, not a command-specific guest exit
interface. The retained logout therefore did not justify a longer process
timeout; guest completion must remain unknown. The exact native waiting
instruction was not captured, so source review is not a native stack diagnosis.

The isolated offline correction keeps framing, client result and guest status
separate. Its preflight refuses process-completion use of that console and any
unreviewed fallback. Eight focused controls and 25 existing orchestration
controls pass without executing WSL. No replacement executor was activated, no
marker was promoted into retirement proof and the original timeout stayed
intact. A future finite exchange needs its own process-lifetime contract.

The root metadata already exists, so repeating the lookup would not advance the
current investigation. The next independent decision is clock policy for the
shared time namespace, not another wrapper around debug-shell. Correcting the
measurement interface does not correct the clock writers or open original
delivery, fault qualification or a server run.

### Isolate the test clock domain before changing shared services

The [clock-policy proposal](../testing/performance/0.74/wsl-clock-policy-options-20261023.md)
compares leaving WSL unchanged, pausing one visible daemon, coordinating the
whole WSL time domain and moving functional fault tests to an independent Linux
kernel. The recorded writers and root metadata do not justify treating Ubuntu
timesyncd as the only control. The already applied kernel discipline also cannot
be assumed to disappear when a daemon stops.

The recommendation is to leave shared WSL time untouched and first evaluate a
separate local Linux VM. This is a risk/isolation choice, not evidence that a VM
automatically has good clocks: its time service and host integration still need
review and admission. A different WSL distro or ordinary container does not
provide the proposed boundary; Linux time namespaces do not virtualize
CLOCK_REALTIME. [Linux time namespace semantics](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/time_namespaces.7.html)

The next permission boundary is only a read-only feasibility inventory. Creating
the environment, observing its clocks and running original-owner/fault cells
are distinct later approvals. The original live checks and 300/60/10-second
windows remain unchanged, and old WSL context pins cannot be transplanted to a
new kernel. Functional fault coverage on a VM would not supply bare-metal
performance or continuous-retention qualification. This separates infrastructure
readiness from product readiness without making the first refusals disappear.

### A healthy clock control does not close a preparation budget failure

The operator then selected the [bounded dedicated-Linux control](../testing/performance/0.74/native-clock-and-holder-result-20261023.md)
instead of creating a local VM. The same standalone observer retained all 601
rows without sampled backward or libc/syscall bracket anomalies. No clocks or
time services were changed. That finite result justified only proceeding to the
preregistered limited holder test, not asserting permanent clock health.

The unchanged GNU image still failed its first healthy case. Its original
BOOTTIME origin was already 9.027 seconds old at the first custody observation;
owned-root preparation reached an expiry at 10.015 seconds. The kernel refusal
field was null, while the causal record explicitly said expired. The matrix
stopped before its four intended fault cases. This is a different first result
from the earlier WSL clock-order failures, not a replacement for them.

The lesson is narrower than blaming a clock or a single expensive check. Age
records locate a preparation budget problem but do not separate CPU, filesystem
work and scheduling. They call for attribution before another isolated change,
not extending the window, reissuing an origin or running healthy until it passes.
Systemd FD compatibility is another future gate, not the cause recorded here.

Supervisor, boot, installed hashes and checked marker state remained unchanged,
and postflight confirmed the checked fixture cleanup and mount-table equality.
Those successful safety checks are retained beside the failed matrix; they do
not turn it into all-writer or original-delivery proof. The next optimization
must preserve both facts: the environment control passed, and preparation still
did not fit the original admission window.

### Validation rather than waiting dominates output preparation

A [separate instrumented native case](../testing/performance/0.74/native-preparation-attribution-result-20261024.md)
kept the same image, source inputs, live predicates and original windows. Output
preparation took 7.155 seconds wall and 7.077 seconds CPU in the current process.
Its 46 ReservedLive steps accounted for 6.049 seconds wall. This is one diagnostic
observation, not a repeated improvement estimate or a measurement of child CPU.

The nested kernel-context span was 4.016 seconds. Its Origin children include
153,088 Boot observations and 306,176 Namespace observations. These spans
overlap: adding them would count the same work several times. Nor can the small
wall-minus-process-CPU difference be labelled I/O wait without a separate trace.
The result supports targeting work inside fresh validation, while keeping every
required observation. It does not justify deleting a check because it is costly.

One bounded hypothesis is indexing the five relevant status fields in a single
pass over each newly read document. The candidate must preserve duplicate-field
refusals and the old parsing order, and cannot cache status bytes between reads.
Leaf timing and differential tests must decide whether that mechanism helps;
they cannot establish the full preparation margin by extrapolation. The profile
itself still expired during owned-root preparation. Its clean postflight and
unchanged supervisor are safety evidence, not a successful execution gate.

### Indexing fresh status fields reduces parser CPU without caching observations

The [isolated status-parser candidate](../testing/performance/0.74/status-field-scan-result-20261024.md)
replaces five text scans with one short-lived field index. It still validates
the same newly read bytes, parses fields in the old order and rejects duplicates
at the same logical point. Nothing is cached between reads. Seeded differential
tests include multiple simultaneous errors, because a parser can reject the
same invalid input while accidentally changing which failure is observed first.

Five matched GNU 1.94 pairs pass the fixed pure-parser CPU gate. The upper
95-percent candidate/baseline bounds are 0.2805, 0.3180 and 0.2358 for three
synthetic document shapes. These ratios belong to the extracted parser control,
not the whole native validation round or product throughput. The native profile
also contains filesystem, namespace, authority and other work; multiplying its
old spans by the new leaf ratios would manufacture an unmeasured total gain.
Current/MSRV kernel and filesystem controls pass without changing read counts
or the original admission windows. A full preparation margin is still unproved.

Expanded checks uncovered a separate integration problem: historical source
preservation tests were comparing later bootstrap additions with older snapshots.
The independent baseline also fails. Keeping those first failures matters as
much as keeping a negative timing result. A historical predecessor view is valid
only after checking the complete current input against an explicit reviewed
version; it cannot be a permissive exclusion of inconvenient code. The new parser
has its own raw-current mutation guard, while the still-red integrated source
gate is repaired separately. Neither a fast leaf nor a clean local build opens
original delivery, writer retirement or production enrollment by itself.

### Repair source views, then distinguish test interference from runtime faults

The [complete source-contract repair](../testing/performance/0.74/source-guard-and-ordinary-entry-result-20261024.md)
now passes all 321 selected assertions without filtering. Exact current versions
are checked before historical bodies are supplied, and normalization order is
corrected; no runtime predicate or observation frequency changes. A first six-case
repair failure and a duplicate-module Clippy refusal remain in the archive.

The broader ordinary regression is independently red: 1465 passes, sixteen
failures and 141 ignored cases. Six fixtures sign an old lock digest while
supplying the current lock. Two descriptor oracles assume an otherwise idle
process, although tests run beside unrelated opens and forks. Owned controls
show why a CLOEXEC writer can still delay EOF after fork and why a thread's
procfs FD directory includes other threads' files. These explain possible
interference, not the identity of an unobserved historical competitor.

GNU entry/API controls pass, while the first MSRV current-image cohort retains
three ETXTBSY refusals. Repeating or serializing until green would not resolve
the oracle's scope. The next candidate must isolate only the FD-sensitive case,
preserve its actual assertions and deadlines, and prove exact child selection,
bounded owned cleanup and no retry. Kernel/time failures remain separately open;
a test-harness correction must not be presented as production writer retirement.

### Reuse immutable history without caching live observations

A separate [source-test cache](../testing/performance/0.74/historical-source-cache-result-20261024.md)
retains complete blobs by full Git commit ID and path. Its controlled loader
runs once for repeated or concurrent same-key callers, while every current file
is still read and validated anew. It cannot cache credentials, policy or kernel
facts, and lives in the source-test process rather than a measured process.
All 321 old assertions remain selected and passing. Two unpaired suite times
are retained as observations, not advertised as a repeatable speedup.

The ordinary RESP/client-surface tests also pass independently. That establishes
their checked correctness, not a throughput floor or acceptance of any rejected
product hypothesis. Source checks, fixture corrections, performance evidence and
actual launch authority remain different gates even when all are needed for the
same release.

### Correct the fixture without weakening the verifier

The [ordinary repair](../testing/performance/0.74/ordinary-repair-result-20261024.md)
tested a plausible but wrong fix: bind a newly signed fixture receipt to the
current root lock. The independent production input pin still rejected it on
both compilers. That rejection was useful evidence, not a reason to change the
pin. The accepted fixture correction supplies the exact historical lock bytes
already named by the original receipt. New negative controls show that a valid
synthetic signature over another digest still cannot override the independent
pin. A signature proves who asserted bytes; it does not make arbitrary bytes
part of the approved build.

Descriptor and busy-executable tests needed a different correction. Their old
assertions were sound only within an owned process scope, not beside unrelated
forking tests. A narrow exact-case subprocess keeps those bodies intact while
the parent suite remains parallel. Its controls reject zero selected tests,
wrong/nonzero outcomes, timeout and surviving descendants; cleanup is never
counted as successful retirement. The intentional ETXTBSY negative control
continues holding its writer and requiring refusal.

These repairs do not make the whole suite green. Both complete ordinary cohorts
retain failures, and their logs record backwards REALTIME under an unchanged
boot ID. A later passing name does not explain an earlier failing one. Parallel
log adjacency also cannot tie every clock event to a particular test. Preserve
the first results, classify only what the saved data proves and keep original
clock predicates active.

The [remaining release boundaries](../testing/performance/0.74/release-closure-audit-20261024.md)
are consequently explicit: a parser CPU win, correct fixtures and source tests
do not establish full preparation fit, authenticated worker execution, cessation
of every writer, durable completion or production trust. Local correctness,
ownership proof, performance acceptance and authority to operate the host are
separate gates. Moving one forward must not silently waive the others.
